analysis.one_liner: Bars federal judges from owning individual stocks and applies an enforceable ethics code to the Supreme Court.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or committee vote; it died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, with 30 Democratic cosponsors and none from the other party.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal judges and Supreme Court justices could no longer own individual stocks, hedge funds, derivatives, or stakes in private companies — only diversified funds, government bonds, personal homes, retirement accounts, and a new Treasury-run investment account. The bill would have extended the enforceable Code of Conduct to the nine Supreme Court justices, who have never been bound by it as lower-court judges are, created a House-appointed committee to review misconduct complaints against them, and required public recusal lists, filed speeches, and online audio of arguments. It also banned gifts of travel, lodging, and meals tied to privately sponsored judicial seminars and limited courts' power to seal evidence or enforce secret settlements in public-health-and-safety cases. It followed years of reporting on judges who ruled in cases involving companies whose stock they owned.
analysis.who_benefits: Every litigant in federal court would face judges without personal stakes in the outcome; parties and whistleblowers in product-safety, pollution, and public-health cases would stop losing hazard evidence to sealed settlements; and journalists and court watchers would get searchable recusal lists, filed speeches, online audio of arguments, and public misconduct data.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Anyone with a case in federal court

how_it_helps.text: Removes personal financial conflicts: judges and justices could no longer own individual stocks, bonds, commodities, futures, hedge funds, derivatives, or stakes in private businesses, and could not sit on for-profit boards — only diversified widely held funds, government bonds, personal residences, retirement accounts, and a new Treasury-run investment account would be allowed.

Puts teeth behind the rules: the Attorney General or Special Counsel could sue violators for civil penalties of up to $50,000 per violation, and the enforceable Code of Conduct for U.S. Judges would apply to Supreme Court justices to the same extent as other federal judges.

Makes recusal checkable: judges would file public, searchable lists of every association or interest requiring recusal — including a spouse's or minor child's holdings — and litigants could petition for disqualification, with justices required to respond publicly in writing.

Closes the junket channel: the gift ban would expressly cover transportation, travel, lodging, and meals, with regulations barring gifts connected to privately sponsored judicial seminars; sponsors would have to disclose their litigation activities, and an approved-seminar fund would pay judges' expenses instead.

Keeps hazards public: courts could no longer seal information or enforce confidential settlements in cases involving public health or safety without specific findings, and parties could not be blocked from reporting hazards to regulators.

Opens the courts' own records: contemporaneous online audio of appellate and Supreme Court open sessions, public case-assignment data, filed and posted judicial speeches, and annual public reports on misconduct complaints — including complaints against retired judges, whose retirement or elevation to the Supreme Court would no longer end an inquiry.

analysis.who_pays: Federal judges and Supreme Court justices would divest individual securities and business stakes and face fines of up to $50,000 per violation; companies and foundations that sponsor judicial seminars would lose their gift channel to the bench; taxpayers would fund a new judicial education fund and a complaints committee.

drawbacks.text: The ban reaches nearly every investment class a wealthy judge might hold — stocks, bonds, commodities, futures, hedge funds, derivatives, and private-business stakes — with fines up to $50,000 per violation; critics would argue the burden makes the bench less attractive to qualified people from business, though the bill answers with a Treasury-run account that preserves market exposure.

The Supreme Court complaints committee would sit inside the House of Representatives, its five members appointed by the Speaker and the minority leader, and its findings would force a House Judiciary vote on an impeachment inquiry within 30 legislative days — a design critics would call congressional encroachment on judicial independence, since impeachment is the Constitution's remedy and courts have no parallel power over Congress.

The bill authorizes unlimited appropriations for the new investment accounts and $3 million a year for a fund paying judges' travel, lodging, and meals at approved seminars — a taxpayer-financed perk that replaces sponsor money rather than ending the seminar circuit.

In health-and-safety cases, courts could no longer seal discovery or enforce confidential settlements by default; an honest supporter acknowledges this will lead some defendants to fight longer rather than settle, raising litigation costs even where disclosure serves the public.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real and mostly a good one: judges give up holding shares of companies that may appear before them — softened by a Treasury-run account that preserves market exposure — and in exchange every federal litigant gets a bench without personal stakes, the nine justices face an enforceable code for the first time, and hazard information in health-and-safety cases stops disappearing into sealed settlements. The honest costs: a new taxpayer-funded perk (the seminar fund) and complaints committee, a genuine separation-of-powers question about House appointees policing Supreme Court conduct through a built-in impeachment pipeline, divestiture burdens that could discourage candidates from business careers, and some cases that will cost more to litigate or settle less easily. The conflict-of-interest, transparency, and sealing provisions clearly outweigh these costs; the House committee's mandatory impeachment-vote machinery is the weakest-designed piece.

outcome.mechanism: Referred to six committees and then two subcommittees, the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or floor time, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Pramila Jayapal introduced the bill on May 10, 2022, joined by 13 original cosponsors.

The House sent it to six committees at once — Judiciary, House Administration, Oversight and Reform, Rules, Financial Services, and Agriculture — for periods to be subsequently determined by the Speaker.

On May 19, 2022 it was referred to the Agriculture Committee's subcommittee on commodity exchanges, whose jurisdiction covers the bill's ban on judges trading commodities and futures; on November 1, 2022 it went to the Judiciary Committee's courts subcommittee.
No committee held a hearing or vote on the bill and no floor action ever followed; it expired when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

The bill would have barred federal judges and Supreme Court justices from owning individual stocks, bonds, commodities, futures, hedge funds, derivatives, and stakes in private businesses, with civil fines of up to $50,000 per violation.

It would have applied the Code of Conduct for United States Judges to Supreme Court justices to the same extent as lower-court judges and created complaint procedures, including a five-member review committee appointed by the Speaker and the House minority leader.
It would have required judges to file public, searchable lists of every interest that could force their recusal, including holdings of a spouse or minor child.

It would have tightened the federal gift ban to cover travel, lodging, and meals, barred gifts connected with privately sponsored judicial seminars, and replaced sponsor money with a federal education fund of $3 million a year.
It would have limited courts' power to seal information or enforce secret settlements in cases involving public health or safety, and protected parties' ability to report hazards to regulators.

It would have required online audio of appellate and Supreme Court open sessions, public case-assignment data, filed judicial speeches, annual public misconduct reports, and allowed discipline of retired judges — including reducing their pension benefits — with retirement or elevation to the Supreme Court no longer ending an inquiry.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal judges and Supreme Court justices kept the status quo — personal stock portfolios, no enforceable ethics code for the justices, no outside complaint process — and the companies and foundations that sponsor judicial seminars kept their channel to the bench.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal judges and their seminar sponsors

for.name: Pramila Jayapal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on May 10, 2022 and recruited the original cosponsors

against.name: Jerrold Nadler
against.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill but never scheduled a markup or committee vote during the ten months it sat in his committee

against.name: Nancy Pelosi
against.what_they_did: Left the bill's six-committee referral — whose timing was hers to determine — unsequenced and never gave it floor time before the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Democrat — 30 signed on, none of the chamber's 213 Republicans did — and the bill died in a House that Democrats controlled, so no vote ever tested where the full membership stood.

industries.industry: Federal judges and Supreme Court justices
industries.note: They would have had to divest individual stocks, business stakes, and corporate board seats, file public recusal lists, face fines of up to $50,000 per violation, and answer complaints that could end in an impeachment vote. Their personal financial ties to litigants are exactly what the public interest in impartial courts runs against.

industries.industry: Corporate and foundation sponsors of judicial seminars
industries.note: The gift ban would cover the travel, lodging, and meals these sponsors pay for at private judicial seminars, sponsors would have to disclose their litigation activity, and approved seminars would be paid from a federal fund instead. Seminar sponsorships are a long-standing access channel between interested parties and the bench.

industries.industry: Companies defending public health and safety lawsuits
industries.note: Courts could no longer seal hazard information or enforce confidential settlements by default, and parties could not be barred from telling regulators — more of what these defendants currently pay to keep sealed would become public.

The courts would take on new complaint, disclosure, and reporting duties and submit misconduct data to Congress and the public, while gaining a Treasury fund covering judges' seminar expenses at $3 million a year.
